launches.body:
Hi! We are Lucas and Paul, cofounders of Tire Swing: the AI compliance platform for Affordable Housing.

<https://youtu.be/x4qyhXXz38I>

## **The Problem**

Every Affordable Housing move-in and recertification requires applicant income verification and a strict eligibility review. In addition to the high labor costs and regulatory burden, delays in reviewing applications and thoroughly screening applicants can cause weeks of lost rental revenue.

Lost revenue on a single move-in can accumulate to thousands of dollars, and penalties for non-compliance can cost millions in credit recaptures and fines.

## **The Solution**

Tire Swing uses AI to bring compliance expertise to the point of leasing. It turns weeks of reviews and approvals into a minutes-long process. The platform:

* **Reviews evidence as it is collected.** Tire Swing processes documentation in minutes, allowing problems to be addressed before the applicant leaves the office.
* **Performs the eligibility analysis.** It calculates household income, applies all applicable property, state, and program eligibility rules, and links every finding to its supporting evidence.
* **Automates certification compliance.** Tire Swing flags missing, inconsistent, or incorrect information with steps to resolve the problem from a library of thousands of deterministic and AI driven compliance checks.

**Tire Swing means faster move-ins and recertifications, reduced consulting budget, and more consistent, audit-ready files.** 

## **Looking ahead**

We believe Affordable Housing is the first application of a much larger needs-based eligibility opportunity. Federal, state, and local governments distribute more than $1.5 trillion annually through needs-based programs including Medicaid, SNAP, TANF, utility assistance, and tax credits.

These programs share a common underlying workflow: collect documents, convert them into structured facts, apply eligibility rules, and resolve missing or contradictory information.  The administration costs for these services are approximately $20B annually.

## **The Team**

Tire Swing is founded by Paul and Lucas, college friends and Princeton computer science graduates. Prior to founding Tire Swing, Lucas worked as a software engineer at Instacart and Capital One, and Paul worked as a cybersecurity consultant at Stroz Friedberg.

name: Definite
long_description:
Definite is where finance teams build everyday back-office agents on one live model of their books. We plug into your ERP, ledger, payroll, and payments read-only and compile everything into one clean model that stays current as money moves. Your back-office team then builds agents on top in plain English. We never write back and we never move money. The agents are yours, the plumbing is ours.

We met in first year computer science at Waterloo and interned at Meta, Optiver, and BitGo. At Optiver they ran an n8n hackathon and the interns automated basically nothing. It couldn't talk to the systems that mattered. When we pitched banks and fintechs on agents, they kept telling us the same thing. The agent isn't the hard part, getting clean data out of their systems is.

Right now, automating anything in a back office means engineers hand-stitching data from a dozen sources in different formats on different schedules. Tools like n8n and Workato assume your data is already clean and joined. In finance it never is. So the teams with the most repetitive work and smallest budgets get nothing.

The hard part is the compiler. Every source gets cleaned, matched, and joined into one live model of transactions, invoices, vendors, and payments, and it has to stay right as money lands every day. 

Everyone throws engineers at this. We're doing it once so nobody has to again. Every back office is getting agents eventually. Whoever owns the data they read from owns the thing all of them depend on, and eventually the books themselves. That's what we're building.

launches.body:
_AI agents that run the entire regulatory reporting pipeline for banks, from raw ledger data to the filed report._

**_TL;DR_**_: Definite automates regulatory reporting for banks end to end, from raw ledger data to filed report, turning weeks of manual work into hours._ [usedefinite.com](http://usedefinite.com)

Hey! We're Gurshabd, Mazin and Farhan from Definite.

<https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ji1ae8y_V4E>

**The Problem**

Proving to regulators that their books follow the rules is a constant, non-negotiable obligation for banks. Each report is thousands of numbers, personally signed off by an executive. Getting it wrong can mean a **fine up to a million dollars** over a single undetected error. Producing that proof is slow, and doesn't even guarantee it's correct. 

Here's where the current system breaks down:

1. **Wasted Hours:** A controller pulls data from the core system into Excel and maps it line by line by hand. By regulators' own estimate, one quarterly filing takes weeks of employee time, time pulled from higher-value finance work every quarter.
2. **False Confidence:** The software banks use to file checks formatting, not truth. A loan mapped to the wrong schedule line sails through every check. Nothing catches it until an examiner does, and by then it's not a mistake, it's a violation.

**The Solution**

**Report agents:** We connect to your books and our agents build the reports you owe.

**Verification engine:** Every number is recomputed from source records and checked against a versioned rulebook, so each line carries its rule and source data.

**Self-correcting agents:** When a check fails, the agent gets the reason and fixes it in seconds. Real exceptions come to your team with a drafted explanation, not a blank error. This loop is why our agents are the most accurate in finance.

**Receipts:** Every check produces a tamper-evident receipt you can hand an examiner or auditor.

Your team reviews and signs instead of building.

**How we got here**

Gurshabd worked at BitGo, a regulated crypto custodian, where attestations proving customer assets matched the ledger were built by hand every period. Farhan worked at Meta where he delved extensively into machine learning and building AI agents. Mazin saw Optiver recheck daily regulatory numbers by hand, then built LLM agents at [Boosted.ai](http://Boosted.ai) and learned finance people won't act on AI output unless every number comes with its source.

The lesson from all three: in finance, producing a number is cheap, proving it is the job. On two public reporting benchmarks, DeepSeek V3 with our verification engine outperformed GPT-5 on reconciliation accuracy (FinBalance) at roughly 50× lower cost, and beat the entire published field on XBRL calculation validation (FinAuditing).

launches.body:
**TL;DR: Veltha reads an entire claim file, flags what's missing, and applies the exact federal regulation that governs it, producing a citation-backed determination a human adjuster just signs off on. Work that took an adjuster \~6 hours now takes \~10 minutes.** Starting with workers' comp and crop insurance.

<https://www.loom.com/share/9e9701f61bf4400890b4799fdda3d3ff>

**The problem**

1 in 4 claims adjusters expect to retire within five years. Experienced adjusters are retiring faster than carriers can replace them, and processing capacity is now the binding constraint on growth.

**What we built**

Veltha is an AI claims adjuster that runs the whole file end to end:

* **Triage** - reads incoming claim emails and documents, classifies them, and routes each claim to the right workflow.
* **Gap detection** - checks the file for missing documents and records, then requests them by email, phone, or fax and runs follow-up cadences until they land.
* **Compliance review** - applies the relevant federal rulebook, and produces a determination where **every output element is tied to a source span and a specific regulatory provision.**

The adjuster's job shifts from _doing_ the claim to _reviewing_ Veltha's output. Less chasing. Faster decisions. Output that survives an audit.

**What we understand that others don't: regulation is the moat, not the obstacle.** Horizontal platforms (Guidewire, Duck Creek) and generic AI-claims startups can summarize a claim file. They can't tell you _which_ provision triggered _which_ adjustment, with citations. We treat the federal rulebook as an anchor for the workflow we embed within the organisation. That's the difference between a summary a human re-does from scratch and an output an adjuster will actually sign.

**Our ask**

name: herdr
long_description:
Developers don't run one coding agent anymore. They run fleets of them — for hours, sometimes days — across laptops, servers, and sandboxes. Keeping track of that work is the new bottleneck: which agent is blocked, which one finished, which terminal is it in, and why did everything die when the laptop closed.

Herdr is the open-source home for that work. A background server owns the agents' terminal sessions on each machine, so the work survives disconnects, closed lids, and dropped SSH. Herdr detects each agent and turns the chaos into an attention queue — working, blocked, done, across every project — so you look only when an agent needs you. Every client is just a view: the bundled terminal UI, SSH from another machine, your phone. Close one, open another; the work never stops.

Software can drive it too: a CLI, a socket API, and a plugin marketplace that passed 500 community plugins in its first month. The runtime is Apache-2.0 and stays open. Four months after launch: 25k GitHub stars, 340k downloads.

name: Sentient OS
long_description:
Nobody's built truly proactive AI, because it requires running inference on your entire life. In the cloud, that's insanely expensive and a privacy nightmare. But not on your own chip.

Every night, Sentient's on-device LLM wakes your Mac and understands what's new in your life (email, messages, files, Granola transcripts...), entirely locally, and distills it into a knowledge base.

You wake up to your work already prepared: the reply you forgot, drafted from your own context; the subscription you never use renewing tomorrow, caught; the report you promised in the group chat, ready to send. Everything is one click from firing through computer use, and nothing fires until you click.

Or click your Mac notch anytime and say "finish this for me." Sidekick takes over the thing you were doing with its own cursor while you move on.

On-device inference at this scale was supposed to be impossible: devices too slow, and models too dumb. So we built the stack ourselves: a custom LiteRT-LM fork (KV-cache reuse, speculative decoding, custom k-quants) that runs nightly on 8 GB Macs. The user's hardware does ~90% of the compute, and their own ChatGPT or Claude subscription does the rest, so our marginal cost is ~$0, and our servers store nothing.

Our alpha soft-launch was top post of the month on r/macapps (688 upvotes), and we launched to 4000+ users in our first week with $0 marketing. We're free and open source for consumers; the same engine on the work stack (Slack, Granola, Linear, Notion) is the enterprise business.

Sentient OS raised ~$1M in pre-seed, backed by YC, Afore, and the a16z Speedrun scout fund.

name: Hemlock
long_description:
Every serious robotics lab is bottlenecked on the same thing: demonstration data. The field has converged on egocentric video and hand pose as the substrate, and both are now cheap to collect at scale. What neither of them contains is force. A video of someone picking up an egg and a video of someone picking up a rock are nearly identical in pixel space and nearly identical in joint angles. They differ almost entirely in a quantity nobody is recording. Policies trained without it learn geometry and inherit no sense of touch.

Hemlock closes that gap at the source. Our device, the Bracelet, is a wrist-worn surface EMG band that reads the electrical activity of the forearm muscles that actually drive the hand, which means it recovers contraction force directly rather than inferring it from motion. This distinction is the whole thesis: force cannot be reconstructed downstream of kinematics, because a hand squeezing hard isometrically and a hand resting can occupy the identical pose. Muscle signal is the only non-invasive channel that separates them.
one_liner: Force-sensing wristband for training robotic AI

launches.body:
**TL;DR: We're 40-50% faster than existing cloud providers in serving frontier robot AI models, e.g. DreamZero, MolmoAct2.**

<https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jVqvJFBRcd0>

\[1x speed, autonomous\]

DSL is building the fastest cloud inference platform for robotics. We let you deploy physical AI without needing expensive local GPUs.

Robot foundation models are growing more and more computationally expensive. The latest frontier of robotics no longer fits feasibly on local GPUs. Compute costs keep soaring amidst a global LPDDR shortage; NVIDIA just doubled the prices of Jetsons in July.

**We're taking a contrarian bet that the future is moving inference _off the robot_ and _into the cloud._**

![uploaded image](/media/?type=post&id=115448&key=user_uploads/3499827/4ca20fc9-00a8-4043-bc43-d51b8b5d0cbf)

How do we do this? We work across the full stack of robot inference to push latency down:

* Model-level architectural adjustments for faster inference
* Kernel-level optimizations to maximally leverage server-grade GPUs
* Network-level optimizations for fast and reliable transport over the cloud
* Region-specific compute allocation to ensure the shortest physical distance between the servers and our customers' robots

These optimizations enable us to be **8% faster** than NVIDIA's implementation **at half the GPU count** (320ms vs 350ms, for DreamZero 14B).

![uploaded image](/media/?type=post&id=115448&key=user_uploads/3499827/69393040-ca17-41cd-a1fb-cd5d70176921)

Furthermore, something we noticed for robotics companies with fast R&D cycles was that their GPUs had long idle periods with concentrated bursts of inference traffic. We're one of the first companies in the world to offer on-demand pricing for physical AI inference, giving users more flexibility with the cost.

We're already working closely with a range of early partners across deployment, research and evaluation. In full FDE spirit, we collaborate with our customers to custom-fit inference stacks that address their unique deployment challenges. We help you get your robot AI to deployment faster.

Our mission is to democratize access to frontier physical intelligence, and we believe cloud is the way forward. You can read our thesis here:

Hey everyone! 👋 \
\
We're Macy, Faiz and Niyaz - co-founders of[ Papaya](https://papaya.fyi) 

**TL;DR**

Papaya is the optimization engine for AI agents. Connect your production agent and Papaya watches every action, finds what's hurting quality, cost, and latency, and gives you the fix. Once a fix is in place, Papaya makes sure your agent doesn't regress. Teams running Papaya are seeing 20%+ improvements to quality, latency, and cost.

**Ask:** If you run an agent in production, connect it to Papaya. Grab a time to get started [here](https://cal.com/macy-mody/macy-papaya).

<https://youtu.be/cG9iIVB5Psk>

**The Problem**

We’ve been building agentic systems for years (6 years to be exact…before it was cool), including really large ones that helped run major workflows inside Amazon. We know firsthand that the hard part isn’t getting an agent to work, it’s keeping it working at a high quality bar. We consistently saw that every model update and every prompt change shifted behavior in ways nobody caught until something downstream looked wrong. The only way to find out what changed was to pull traces and read them by hand.

Most companies shipping agents today are focused on the next feature for customers and they don't have time to fully maintain what's already been released. When we built our own agent as a three-person team, we hit the same wall. We needed to make sure our agent had high quality answers, was fast for our customers, and as low cost as possible, but we had to look at everything by hand. Every hour we spent examining traces was an hour we couldn’t spend on new product development. That's why we built Papaya.

**How Papaya works 🔧** 

At Papaya, our goal is to do the hard AI engineering work for you, staying up to date on the latest and greatest research so you can take advantage of this knowledge through optimizations. Simply stream your production traces through a lightweight SDK. From there, Papaya:

* **Finds your use cases**: groups every run by the job the agent is doing, so you're looking at "refund requests," not "run 4812."
* **Runs 200+ analyses**: checks every use case against 200+ research-backed failure patterns across quality, cost, and latency.
* **Ranks the fixes by impact**: every recommendation comes with an estimated effect on quality, latency, and cost. Approve the ones you want directly in Papaya and Papaya opens the PR.
* **Watches for regression**: once a fix ships, Papaya keeps checking that the improvement holds.

name: Sona8
long_description:
Sona8 is a voice agent that talks to every employee about how their work gets done. Consulting, transformation and corporate development teams spend a large part of every project on stakeholder interviews and stakeholder alignment, and still only hear from a small share of the people affected.

Each employee gets a link and talks to the agent for about 20 minutes. The agent asks follow-up questions, for example why a step is still done by hand or who else is involved. From the conversations we build process maps and a list of the problems people described, by site and team.

During the implementation, the agent goes back to the employees involved after each initiative and asks whether it was implemented and what changed. The result is a project management office that has talked to every employee. Today consulting firms buy it for the stakeholder interviews at the start of an engagement. Transformation and corporate development teams buy it to run the implementation of a change program.

Over time this becomes the way a company knows how it runs. Sona8 reads the systems the company already uses, connects them to what employees said, and keeps the picture current by asking again. Before a decision, you ask what it would do across sites and teams and get an answer from the whole company. A small team steers a company-wide program that used to need a large one. And AI agents inside the company come here first to learn how the work is done before they change anything.
one_liner: Voice agents that talk to employees enabling transformations

question_answers.question: How did your company get started? (i.e., How did the founders meet? How did you come up with the idea? How did you decide to be a founder?)
question_answers.answer: Thilo and I worked on the same consulting project. We did over 70 stakeholder interviews, then had to manage the stakeholders  during implementation, which meant aligning the same people over and over. In the nights we went running a lot in that time. On one of those runs we started asking what if we automated the whole thing. An AI would be strictly better at every step. It asks better questions because it has heard the other interviews, it analyzes with all the context, and it can go back a month later and ask again.

question_answers.question: What is your long-term vision? If you truly succeed, what will be different about the world?
question_answers.answer:
Every big decision in a company is a choice between alternatives. The alternatives you see depend on the context you have. The context that matters most, how the work is done and where the problems are, sits with thousands of employees and never reaches the people who decide.

If we succeed, that context reaches them. Every employee talks to Sona8, and Sona8 plugs into the ERP, the HR system and the ticketing tools. Together that is a live map of how the company runs, and far more than any team can read. The hard part is finding, out of all of it, what matters for one question, and then adding the atomic insights and the judgment. launches.title: DeepMark - Reinventing Trust in Voice
launches.tagline: A live watermark inside AI voice that survives phone calls
launches.body:
<https://youtu.be/76SqazbxK4w>

Hey, we are Slavko and Kosta 👋

We have been working together for six years, first as two researchers at the University of Montenegro, now as founders. Somewhere along the way, we became best friends. Kosta is our CSO, and I am the CEO.

**The problem**

Voice is uniquely vulnerable to impersonation. A few seconds of audio is enough to clone anyone, and the same voice agents that answer a bank's phone can be turned around and pointed at the bank's customers. People have started to hesitate before picking up. Good technology scales good outcomes, and it scales bad ones just as well. Our job is simple. Restore trust in voice.

**What we built**

DeepMark is real-time audio watermarking for AI voice. When an AI agent speaks, we put a certificate inside the sound itself, on the voice company's side, as the voice is being generated. Not metadata, which gets stripped the moment a file is touched. The certificate becomes part of the voice.

![uploaded image](/media/?type=post&id=116233&key=user_uploads/2023960/b3239118-82c1-4fb4-82c2-f4363685a0be)

Then the voice goes out into the real world, and the real world is rough on audio. Compression, codecs, a bad connection, a cheap speaker, a worse microphone. Think about how flat a human voice sounds over the phone. Our certificate survives the trip. On the other end, a phone, a call center, or an API reads it and shows who is speaking, who issued the certificate, and whether this agent is allowed to be on the line. Detectors ask whether audio is fake. We answer who is authorized to speak.

![uploaded image](/media/?type=post&id=116233&key=user_uploads/2023960/171abdf5-efb9-442b-a153-dbbb1ba981d4)

**Why this is hard**

Four things have to hold at the same time. It has to be real time, or a phone call makes no sense, and voice companies already fight for every millisecond. It has to leave the audio quality alone, nobody trades a worse voice for a safer one. It has to survive the phone line. And the ID has to be long enough, because the longer the ID, the more certificates we can issue. A watermark that works beautifully in the lab falls apart the moment audio meets a phone line. And a live call has no file to sign. Nothing survives the trip except the sound itself, so the identity has to live inside the sound. We spent years hitting that wall. Then we built a tool that measures all four at once and published it, so anyone can check our work, and everyone else's.

![uploaded image](/media/?type=post&id=116233&key=user_uploads/2023960/a9930538-1deb-4609-8938-4bdbcf8c88ce)

**How we got here**

Our mentor, who did his PhD in digital watermarking, told us not to bother. The field was saturated, nothing left to contribute. We were too stubborn to listen, and our learning-based approach turned out to be one of the first of its kind.

Kosta wrote his PhD on watermarking along the way. I am still writing mine! We published some of the earliest work in deep audio watermarking, cited by teams at Meta, Microsoft, Sony, and Adobe. This year our robustness benchmark landed in IEEE Access, and our AWARE paper was accepted at EUSIPCO. Before YC, we signed our first platform license with a leading voice AI provider, and it is now in production.

**Our ask**

We want to meet voice AI companies. If you build voice models, book 20 minutes with us and we will run DeepMark on your own audio, so you can see the mark survive your calls. The EU AI Act's marking rules already apply and the 2 December deadline for systems on the market is close, so this is a good month to talk. If you know someone at a voice AI platform, an intro means a lot to us.

[slavko@deepmark.me](mailto:slavko@deepmark.me), or book a demo at [deepmark.me](http://deepmark.me). Thanks for reading. 🇲🇪 → 🌉
